segments.text: Prologue Prologue In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. They said, "If only a miracle could come down to him from his lord?" Say (O Muḥammad), "Miracles are manifested only by God. I am no more than a warner, clarifier." Is it not enough of a miracle for them that We revealed to you this book which is being recited to them? Indeed, in it there is mercy and a message for those who believe. [29:50-51] These verses from sura Al-‘Ankabūt inform us that the Qur’an is Muḥammad’s miracle. Many other verses throughout the Qur’an state that the Qur’an is a divine scripture whose composition is beyond the literary ability of any other being, be it human or otherwise.
segments.label: page - Prologue

segments.text: Thus, verse number 88 of sura Al-Isrā’ (No. 17) states, “If all the humans and all the jinns banded together to produce a Qur’an like this, they will surely fail, no matter how much assistance they lend one another.” The Qur’an challenges anyone to produce a literary work that exceed or equals the Qur’an’s standard of excellence [2:23], [10:38], [11:13], [52:34].
segments.label: page - Prologue

segments.text: But, it should be pointed out that the miraculous nature of Qur’an is by 1 بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ وَقَالُوا لَوْلَا أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ آيَاتٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ ۖ قُلْ إِنَّمَا الْآيَاتُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ وَإِنَّمَا أَنَا نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ ﴿٥٠﴾ أَوَلَمْ يَكْفِهِمْ أَنَّا أَنْزَلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ يُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ لَرَحْمَةً وَذِكْرَىٰ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ ﴿٥١﴾ قُلْ لَئِنِ اجْتَمَعَتِ الْإِنْسُ وَالْجِنُّ عَلَىٰ أَنْ يَأْتُوا بِمِثْلِ هَٰذَا الْقُرْآنِ لَا يَأْتُونَ بِمِثْلِهِ وَلَوْ كَانَ بَعْضُهُمْ لِبَعْضٍ ظَهِيرًا

segments.text: no means limited to its literary composition. The multidimensional miracle of Qur'an has allowed every generation in the past 14 centuries to witness new miracles in the Qur'an. As the mysteries of the universe are unveiled by advancing science and technology, man discovers that the “new” information has been long established in the Qur'an. Examples of these discoveries include the earth's rotation and movement: “When you look at the mountains, you would think that they are standing still. But they are moving swiftly, just as you see the movement of the clouds. Such is the skillful creation of God, who perfected everything. Surely, He is cognizant of anything you do.” [27:88] Long before it was discovered by man, the Qur'an had stated that the sun is a “source” of light, while the moon is a mere reflection thereof.
segments.label: page

segments.text: This has been mentioned consistently in sura Yūnus [10:5]: “It is He who rendered the sun a lamp, and the moon a light.” and in sura Al-Furqān [25:61]: “Blessed is He who placed in the heaven constellations, and He placed in it a lamp, and a lighted moon,” and in sura Nūh [71:16]: “And He rendered the moon in (the heaven) a light, and He rendered the sun a Lamp.” 2 وَتَرَى الْجِبَالَ تَحْسَبُهَا جَامِدَةً وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحَابِ ۚ صُنْعَ اللَّهِ الَّذِي أَتْقَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ ۚ إِنَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِمَا تَفْعَلُونَ هُوَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ ضِيَاءً وَالْقَمَرَ نُورًا تَبَارَكَ الَّذِي جَعَلَ فِي السَّمَاءِ بُرُوجًا وَجَعَلَ فِيهَا سِرَاجًا وَقَمَرًا مُنِيرًا وَجَعَلَ الْقَمَرَ فِيهِنَّ نُورًا وَجَعَلَ الشَّمْسَ سِرَاجًا
segments.label: page

segments.text: Prior to the discovery that the Pharaohs' bodies were preserved, the Qur'an indicated that the ancient Egyptians were endowed with the hitherto unknown science of mummification. They were given such knowledge in order to preserve the body of the anti-Moses Pharaoh, and set him up as an example for subsequent generations. This revelation is in sura Yūnus (10:92): "We will preserve your body to render you an example for subsequent generations." The body of anti-Moses Pharaoh is currently on display at the Cairo Museum. Equally miraculous is the total absence from the Qur'an of nonsense statements. The Qur'an was revealed in an era dominated by ignorance, superstition, and a multitude of absurd beliefs. For example, it was widely believed that the earth was carried on the horns of a giant bull. When the bull switched from one horn to the other, this caused earthquakes.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Despite the predominance of this and similar beliefs, the Qur'an does not contain any statements disproven by modern science. The miracles of previous messengers of God which are narrated in the Bible and the Qur'an were visually perceptible performances witnessed by a few contemporaneous individuals. For example, how many people actually saw the staff of Moses (peace be upon him) turn into a snake? How many people actually saw Jesus Christ (peace be upon him) revive the dead, and create birds from clay? 3 فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً
segments.label: page

segments.text: Since the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the final messenger, it is only logical that his miracle should be a perpetual one. (Of course, all miracles belong to God. It is in relative context only that we speak of the prophets' miracles.) The Qur'an is a mental miracle which is continuously witnessed by those fortunate enough to gain access to it. [As mentioned in sura Al-An'am (6:25), sura Al-Isra' (17:46), sura Al-Kahf (18:57), and sura Al-Waqi'a (56:77-79), the Qur'an is not available to just anyone who reads it. One has to be sincere and impartial if the Qur'an is to be made available to him] Thus, the miracle of Muhammad (peace be upon him) has been witnessed by his own generation; it is being witnessed by the present generation; and it will be witnessed by every subsequent generation till the Day of Judgement.
segments.label: page

segments.text: A prerequisite for this perpetual witnessing of the Qur'an's miracle is that it must be preserved. For this reason, God Almighty Himself vowed in sura Al-Hijr (15:9) to preserve His final message: "We have revealed this message, and, surely, We will preserve it." Of all divine scriptures, ONLY the Qur'an remains unaltered. Today, we can buy the Qur'an in Tokyo, Cairo, Washington, or Karachi, and find all these copies identical with each other, and identical with the Quran preached by Muhammad (peace be upon him) and recited by him as he led the prayers 14 centuries ago. One of the unique features of the Qur'an is the occurrence at the beginning of certain suras of alphabets إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحَافِظُونَ
segments.label: page

segments.text: which bear no apparent meanings. These alphabets, henceforth called “Qur’anic Initials,” are not known in any other literary work. The study of the Qur’anic initials which is reported in this book is another demonstration of the eternal nature of Muḥammad’s miracle, the Quran. 5

segments.text: Chapter 1: Prerequisite Information About The Qur'an Chapter 1 Prerequisite Information About The Qur'an To derive maximum benefit from this study, a review of some basic information about the Qur'an is required. Since we will be dealing with many words and alphabetic letters of the Arabic language, a convention for the pronunciation and transliteration of the Arabic alphabet is presented in Table 1. The Qur'an is made up of 114 chapters (suras) of varied lengths. Each sura consists of a number of verses ranging from 3 [suras Al-‘Aṣr (no. 103), Al-Kawthar (108), and Al-Naṣr (110)] to 286 verses [sura Al-Baqara (no. 2)].
segments.label: page - Chapter 1: Prerequisite Information About The Qur'an

segments.text: The location of revelation of each sura is designated as “Meccan” or “Medinan.” All suras revealed before Hijra (the Prophet’s migration from Mecca to Medina) are considered “Meccan,” while those revealed after Hijra are considered “Medinan,” regardless of the exact location of revelation. Recording of the Qur'anic suras follows a specific sequence which is different from the revelation order. Table 2 lists the suras according to their recording sequence. The chronological sequence, i.e., the revelation sequence is shown in Table 3. The location of revelation of each sura is shown in both tables.
segments.label: page - Chapter 1: Prerequisite Information About The Qur'an

segments.text: There has always been one version of the Qur'an, recorded during the lifetime of the Prophet Muḥammad (peace be upon him). The slightest alteration or distortion of this one version renders it Qur'an no more. Since the Prophet was keenly aware of the distortions which afflicted previous scriptures, he instructed the writers of God's revelation never to write anything from him except those Qur'anic revelations. He made it clear to them that this was but one precaution against the accidental injection of non-Qur'anic material into God's message. The Prophet personally supervised the recording and organization of the Qur'an down to the individual verses within each sura.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Zeid ibn Thābit, the foremost revelation writer and a constant companion of the Prophet, is reported by Al-Bukhāry and other sources of Hadīth as saying, “We used to be with the messenger of God (peace be upon him) when we wrote the Qur'an on sheets. Whenever a verse, or a number of verses, was revealed, the Prophet would say, 'Put this verse here, and that verse there,' exactly as (the angel) Gabriel had taught him, in accordance with the will of God Almighty.” Evidence for the existence of the Qur'an, as we know it today, during the Prophet's life is abundant.
segments.label: page

segments.text: For instance, the classic references of Al-Ḥākim, Ibn Khuzeima, Ibn Majah, and Al-Bayhaqy, report that the Prophet said, “After the death of a believer, certain of his righteous deeds continue to yield credit for him: the knowledge he had taught to others, pious offspring whom he left behind, and the Qur'an inherited from him.” This 14
segments.label: page

segments.text: inherited Qur’an is understood to be in the physical form of a book, or in the intangible form of memory. Recitation of the Qur’an by the Prophet as he led the prayers is reported by numerous companions, and is shown to be identical to the Qur’an in existence today. Al-Bukhārī gives the following account for the recording of the Qur’an: “It was ‘Umar ibn Al-Khaṭṭāb who became concerned about the possible loss of the Qur’an. In the battle of Yamāma, ‘Umar witnessed the falling of a number of martyrs who had the Qur’an committed to their memories. ‘Umar then alerted the Khalīfa Abū Bakr, first successor to the Prophet, and he too became concerned. ‘Umar and Abū Bakr called Zeid ibn Thābit, widely known as the Prophet’s secretary, and asked him to collect the Qur’an and write it down in one unit to serve as a permanent reference.
segments.label: page

segments.text: About this assignment, Zeid said, ‘In view of the awesome responsibility entrusted to me, it would have been an easier task had the Khalīfa commanded me to move a mountain. I went around collecting the very original writings of Qur’an which had been transcribed on pieces of leather, wood, bones, and rocks, as well as from the memories of men. The collected materials were checked against each other for accuracy.’ After completing his assignment, Zeid handed the recorded Qur’an over to Abū Bakr. When Abū Bakr died, the second Khalīfa, ‘Umar, took charge of this Qur’an. When ‘Umar, died, his daughter Ḥafṣa, a widow of the Prophet, kept the original recorded Quran. During the reign of ‘Uthmān 15
segments.label: page

segments.text: ibn ‘Affān, one of his emissaries to Syria and Iraq, named Ḥuzeifa ibn Al-Yamān, came to him and informed him of serious variations in reciting the Qur’an by the Muslims of Syria and Iraq. Ḥuzeifa said to ‘Uthmān ‘O prince of the faithful, save this nation before they distort their scripture as the Christians and Jews have distorted theirs.’ ‘Uthman immediately sent for the Qur’an from Ḥafṣa, and ordered the reproduction thereof. Four of the original revelation writers were charged with the reproduction work. They were Zeid ibn Thābit, ‘Abdullah ibn Al-Zubair, Sa‘īd ibn Al-‘Aṣ and ‘Abdul-Raḥmān ibn Al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām. The reproduced copies were dispatched to Baṣra (Iraq), Kūfa (Iraq), Damascus (Syria), and Mecca. Other copies were kept in Medina.” These copies were further reproduced and they represent the originals for the Qur’an published today. 16
segments.label: page

segments.text: Chapter 2: The Qur'anic Initials Chapter 2 The Qur'anic Initials Of the 114 suras in the Qur'an, 28 begin with one set of Qur'anic initials, and one sura is prefixed with two sets of Qur'anic initials. Each set of Qur'anic initials consists of a number of letters ranging between one and five. The different sets of Qur'anic initials and the suras where they occur are listed in Table 4. As shown in that table, there are 14 different sets of Qur'anic initials, and the number of letters which participate in the make-up of these initials is also 14. The 14 letters involved in the formation of Qur'anic initials are Alif (A), Ḥā (Ḥ), Rā (R), Sīn (S), Ṣād (Ṣ), Ṭā (Ṭ), ‘Ayn (‘A), Qāf (Q), Kāf (K), Lām (L), Mīm (M), Nūn (N), Hā (H), and Yā (Y).
segments.label: page - Chapter 2: The Qur'anic Initials

segments.text: These letters are known in the Muslim literature, more specifically among the Sufi mystics, as “the illumination letters الحُرُوف النُّورَانِيَّة .” The other half of the alphabet, the 14 letters not involved, are known as “the darkness letters الحُرُوف الظُّلْمَانِيَّة .” To explain the reasoning behind this nomenclature, we would have to go beyond the scope of this book. The suras which contain Qur'anic initials are listed in their recorded sequence in Table 5. The same suras, listed in their chronological (revelation) sequence, are shown in Table 6. As we shall see later, both sequences are important in the final analysis of the Qur'anic initials. 17 الحُرُوف النُّورَانِيَّة الحُرُوف الظُّلْمَانِيَّة

segments.text: Chapter 3: REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE Chapter 3 REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE During the past 14 centuries, a number of theories were developed dealing with the possible significance of the Qur’anic initials. The most comprehensive reviews of these theories are those reported by Al-Suyūṭy’s famous reference, “Al-Itqān Fī ‘Ulūm Al-Qur’an,” and Al-Bayḍāwy in his well-known commentary on the Qur’an. There is an unanimous agreement among the Muslim scholars who studied the Qur’anic initials that these “mysterious” letters have something to do with the miraculous nature of the Qur’an. Most of those scholars considered the magnificent literary composition of the Qur’an, and the fact that it was revealed through an illiterate man (the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him), to be the miracle of the Qur’an.
segments.label: page - Chapter 3: REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

segments.text: Accordingly, it has been generally believed that the Qur’an’s frequent challenge for anyone to produce anything like it, is a challenge to compose a literary work as beautiful, precise, and linguistically perfect as the Qur’an. The most predominant theories explaining the Qur’-anic initials can be summarized as follows: 1. The Qur’anic initials represent a challenge for anyone to compose from these alphabets a literary work as awesome as the Qur’an. 2. The Qur’anic initials were placed at the beginning of certain suras to attract the listeners’ attention. 21
segments.label: page - Chapter 3: REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

segments.text: APPENDIX I. The Abbreviated Letters (Al-Muqatta'āt) 3. The Qur'anic initials are secret or symbolic names of God. 4. The Qur'anic initials are symbolic names of the suras where they occur. 5. The Qur'anic initials are secret or symbolic names of the Qur'an, similar to Al-Furqān and Al-Dhikr. 6. The Qur'anic initials are words in a foreign tongue. Al-Bayḍāwy, however, dismissed this theory on the basis that the Qur'an repeatedly states that it was revealed in a "perfect Arabic tongue." 7. Ibn 'Abbās theorized that the letter Alif (A) in Alif Lām Mīm stands for Allāh (God), the Lām (L) stands for the angel Gabriel, and the Mīm (M) stands for Muḥammad. Thus, this set of Quranic initials informs us that the Qur'an came from God to the Prophet Muḥammad (peace be upon him), through the mediation of Gabriel. 8.
segments.label: page - APPENDIX I. The Abbreviated Letters (Al-Muqatta'āt)

segments.text: Ibn 'Abbās also combined three different sets of initials, namely, Alif Lām Rā (A.L.R.), Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.), and Nūn (N), to spell out the word Al-Raḥmān, one of God's magnificent names. 9. The most recent and comprehensive study of the Qur'anic initials is that presented by 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali in his Qur'anic translation. His study is reproduced here in its entirety: APPENDIX I. The Abbreviated Letters (Al-Muqatta'āt) Certain Sūras have certain initials prefixed to them, which are called the "Abbreviated Letters". A number of conjectures have been made as to their meaning. Opinions are divided as to the exact meaning of each particular letter or combination of letters, but it is agreed that they have a mystic meaning. 22
segments.label: page - APPENDIX I. The Abbreviated Letters (Al-Muqatta'āt)

segments.text: The 14 letters, which occur in various combinations Mystic meaning, not intelligible at first sight, is not inconsistent with the character of the Qur-ān as a "plain book". The book of nature is also a plain book, but how few can fully understand it? Every one can get out of the Qur-ān plain guidance for his life according to his capacity for spiritual understanding. As his capacity grows, so will his understanding grow. The whole Book is a Record for all time. It must necessarily contain truths that only gradually unfold themselves to humanity. Even parables and tales of mystic meaning employ symbolism. The plain man may find the symbolism helpful, as a soldier finds his National Flag helpful. But what proportion of British soldiers or citizens understands the full symbolism of the British Union Jack?
segments.label: page - The 14 letters, which occur in various combinations

segments.text: This is not a mystery of the same class as "mysteries" by which we are asked to believe against the dictates of reason. If we are asked to believe that one is three and three is one, we can give no intelligible meaning to the words. If we are asked to believe that certain initials have a meaning which will be understood in the fullness of time or of spiritual development, we are asked to draw upon Faith, but we are not asked to do any violence to our reason. I shall try to discuss some of the probable meanings of any particular abbreviated letter or set of abbreviated letters on the first occasion on which it appears in the Qur-ān. But it may be desirable here to take a general view of the facts of their occurrence to help us in appreciating the various views which are held about them.
segments.label: page - The 14 letters, which occur in various combinations

segments.text: There are 29 letters in the Arabic alphabet (counting hamza and alif as two letters), and there are 29 Sūras which have abbreviated letters prefixed to them. One of these Sūras (S. xlii.) has two sets of abbreviated letters, but we need not count this Sūra twice. If we take the half of the alphabet, omitting the fraction, we get 14, and this is the number of letters which actually occur in the Muqaṭṭa'āt.
segments.label: page - The 14 letters, which occur in various combinations

segments.text: The first combination has already been listed under the group of two-letter combinations. This arithmetical analysis brings certain facts into prominence. I do not know how far they have a bearing on the inner meaning of the Muqaṭṭa'āt. The combinations of abbreviated letters that run in a series in consecutive Sūras is noticeable. For example, حم occurs in seven consecutive Sūras from xl. to xlvi. The combination الر occurs in six consecutive Sūras x. to xv., but in one of them (S. xiii.) it is modified to المر, connecting it with the الم series. The الم series covers 6 Sūras. It begins with S. ii. and S. iii., which are practically the beginning of the Qur-ān, and ends with the four consecutive Sūras xxix. to xxxii.

segments.text: I call S. ii. and S. iii. practically the beginning of the Qur-ān, because S. i. is considered a general introduction to the Qur-ān, and the first Sipāra is commonly known as الم, the first verse of S. ii. The combination طسم is prefixed to S. xxvi. and S. xxviii., but the intervening S. xxvii has the combination طس, which may be considered a syncopated form, or the three-letter combination طسم may be considered an extended form of طس. 24 يس حم الم الر طسم المص المر كهيعص حم عسق طس

segments.text: In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said, Again the question arises: Does the ر in الر , المر , and المر , stand for the same signification, or does it mean a different thing in each case? We may generalise and say that there are three series of six, and one series of three, and the others occur all singly. We should logically look for a common factor in the Sūras bearing the same initials, and this factor should be different for Sūras bearing other initials. In all cases where the abbreviated letters occur, there is some mention of the Qur-ān or the Book. The Itqān makes an exception in the case of three Sūras, 'Ankabūt (S. xxix), Rūm (S. xxx), and Nūn (S. lxviii). But a close perusal will show that these Sūras are no exceptions.
segments.label: page - In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said,

segments.text: In xxix. 27 we have a reference to the Book remaining in the family of Abraham, and later on we have a whole Section, (Rukū' No. 5), devoted to the Book, with special reference to the continuity of revelation in the previous Books and the Qur-ān (xxix. 45-51). In xxx. 58 there is express mention of the Qur-ān, and the whole argument of the Sūra leads up to the intimate relation between God's "Signs" in nature (xxx. 20-27) and His revelation in the Qur-ān. In S. lxviii. the very first verse begins the theme with the Pen as the instrument of writing, exhorts Mustafā to stand forth boldly to proclaim the Message, and ends (lxviii. 52) with the declaration that it is a Message for all the worlds. These are general considerations, which I have thought it most convenient to present in the form of an Appendix.
segments.label: page - In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said,

segments.text: In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said, 989. This is a combination of four Abbreviated Letters. For Abbreviated Letters generally, see Appendix I (at the end of Sūra II). The combination here includes the three letters A. L. M., which occurred at the beginning of Sūra II, and are discussed in n. 25 to ii. 1. The additional letter Sād occurs in combination here and in Sūra xix, and by itself at the beginning of S. xxxviii, and nowhere else. The factor common to S. vii, S. xix, and S. xxxviii, is that in each case the core of the Sūra consists in the stories (qisas) of the Prophets. In this Sūra we have the stories of Noah, Hūd, Sālih, Lot, Shu'aib, and Moses, leading up to Muhammad, and in S. xxxviii the stories of David, Solomon, and Job similarly lead up to Muhammad, occupying three out of the five sections.
segments.label: page - In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said,

segments.text: Sūra xix consists almost entirely of such stories. Can we understand Sād to stand for qisas, of which it is the most characteristic letter? In this Sūra vii. we have also the spiritual history of mankind traced,—the Beginning, the Middle, and the End, which, as explained in n. 25, might be represented symbolically by A. L. M. If so, this Sūra, dealing with the Beginning, Middle, and End of man's spiritual story, and illustrating it by the stories of the Prophets, might well be represented symbolically by the letters Alif, Lām, Mīm, Sād. But no one can be dogmatic about these symbols. We must accept them as symbols with a mystic meaning. His explanation of the initials Alif Lām Rā was as follows: As shown in Appendix I (Sipāra 3), the Abbreviated Letters are mystic symbols, about whose meaning there is no authoritative explanation.
segments.label: page - In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said,

segments.text: If the theory advanced in n. 25 to ii. 1 has any validity, and the present group A.L.R. is cognate to the group A.L.M., we have to consider and form some idea in our minds as to the probable meaning of the variation. We took A.L.M. to be a symbol of those Sūras that deal with the beginning, the middle, and the end of man's spiritual history,—the origin, the present position, and the things to come in the Last Days (eschatology, to use a theological term). We took A.L. to stand as symbols of the first two, and M. of the last. In the present group of Sūras we find hardly any eschatological matter, and therefore we can understand the absence of M., the symbol standing for such matter. In its place comes R., which is phonetically allied to L. L. is produced by the impact of the tongue to the front of the palate, and R. to the middle of the palate. In ر, الر, المر, المر
segments.label: page - In his explanation of the Qur'anic initials Alif Lām Mīm Sād, 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali said,

segments.text: The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows: many languages the letters L. and R. are interchangeable; e.g., in Arabic, al-Raḥmān becomes ar-Raḥmān, and R. in imperfect enunciation becomes L., as in Chinese lallations. If L. is a symbol of present-day things looking to the future, we may take R. as a symbol of present-day things looking within, i.e., into the interior of the organization of the Ummat. And this symbolism fits in with the subject-matter of the Sūras in question. But no one should be dogmatic in speculation about mystic Symbols. The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows: 1798. For A.L.M., see ii, 1, n. 25. For A.L.R., see Introduction to S. x. For abbreviated Letters generally see Appendix I. Here there seems to be a combination of the groups A.L.M. and A.L.R.
segments.label: page - The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows:

segments.text: We consider here not only the beginning (A.), the middle (L.), and the end (M.), of man's spiritual history, but also the immediate future of the interior of our organisation, such as it appeared to our Ummat towards the close of the Meccan period. But in trying to understand mystic symbolism, we must not be dogmatic. The befitting attitude is to say: God knows best. As for the letters Kāf Hā Yā‘Ayn Ṣād of sura Maryam (no. 19), A. Y. ‘Ali said, 2455 This is the only Sūra which begins with these five Abbreviated Letters, K. H. Y. 'A. Ṣ For Abbreviated Letters generally, see Appendix I, pp. 118-120. As stated in my note 25, such Letters are Symbols, of which the true meaning is known to God alone. We should not be dogmatic about any conjectures that we make. According to the interpretation of the last letter Ṣād, suggested in n 989 to vii 1.
segments.label: page - The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows:

segments.text: I should be disposed to accept Ṣād with the meaning of Qiṣaṣ, i.e., stories of the Prophets. The main figures referred to here are: Zakariya, Yaḥyā, Maryam, ‘Īsā, and Ibrāhīm: the others are mentioned but incidentally. The strong letter in ZaKariya is K; in IbrāHim, H: in YāḥYā and perhaps MarYam, Y; and in ‘Īsa,—'A (A'in) H also comes in Hārūn (Aaron), and the Arabic Yā comes in all the names including Ismā‘īl and Idrīs. I offer this suggestion with some diffidence. The suggestion of the Tafsīr Kabīr is that the letters stand for attributes of God: K. for Kāfī (the One sufficient in Himself): H for Hādī (He who guides); Y for Yad (Hand as a symbol of Power or Authority Cf. xlviii. 10. "The Hand of God is above their hands"): 'A. for 'Alīm (the All-Knowing); and Ṣ for Ṣādiq (The True One). And in his intoduction to sura Ṭā Hā (Ṭ.
segments.label: page - The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows:

segments.text: H.), he offered the following explanation: The mystic letters Ṭā Hā are prefixed to this Sūra. What do they mean? The earliest tradition is that they denote a dialectical interjection meaning "O man!" If so, the title is particularly appropriate in two ways. (1) It was a direct and personal address to a man in a high state of excitement, tempted by his temper to do grievous wrong, but called by God's Grace, as by a personal appeal, to face the realities, for God knew his inmost secret thoughts (xx. 7): the revelation was sent by God Most Gracious, out of His Grace and Mercy (xx. 5). (2) It takes up the story from the last Sūra, of man as a spiritual being and illustrates it in further details.
segments.label: page - The Alif Lām Mīm Rā at the beginning of sura Al-Ra'ad (no. 13) was explained as follows:

segments.text: It tells the story of Moses in the crisis of his life when he received God's Commission and in his personal relations with his mother, and how he came to be brought up in the Pharaoh's house, to learn all the wisdom of the Egyptians, for use in God's service, and in his personal relations with Pharaoh, whom we take to be his adoptive father (xxviii. 9). It further tells the story of a fallen soul who misled the Israelites into idolatry, and recalls how man's Arch-enemy Satan caused his fall. Prayer and praise are necessary to man to cure his spiritual blindness and enable him to appreciate God's revelation. 26

Thus, the correlation between the Qur'anic initials and the names of God mentioned in the initialed sura was studied. Finally, the decision was made to physically count all the alphabetic letters which make up each one of the Qur'an's 114 suras. segments.text: Chapter 5: METHODS OF CALCULATION Chapter 5 METHODS OF CALCULATION The only calculations carried out manually were the initial determinations of the frequency of occurence of each letter in each sura. A special form was prepared as shown in Figure 1 to facilitate the counting process. As shown in Figure 1, the name of the sura, the number of verses in that sura, its chronological number in the sequence of revelation, and its number in the sequence of recording were listed at the top of the form. The 28 alphabetic letters were listed on the right-hand side of the form on a vertical line. The counting was carried out by reading the sura while placing a short vertical line in front of each letter read.
segments.label: page - Chapter 5: METHODS OF CALCULATION

segments.text: Thus, as بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ was read, a vertical mark was placed in front of the letter Bā, then in front of the letter Sīn, then in front of the letter Mīm, then in front of the letter Alif, then two marks were placed in front of the letter Lām, and so forth. Every fifth mark was a slash across the previous four marks. When a sura was completed, the number of each letter was obtained by counting the marks in front of it, and the total number of alphabetic letters was calculated by adding up the numbers of all 28 letters. The final result for sura Al-Fātiḥa (no. 1) is illustrated in Figure 2. All subsequent calculations were carried out by means of a Xerox Data System's Sigma 7 electronic computer, utilizing a teletype terminal (Time-Share 31 بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ
segments.label: page - Chapter 5: METHODS OF CALCULATION

segments.text: Network). All programing was done in FORTRAN IV language. A library program of Com-Share, Inc. entitled “MARS” was used for the arrangement of the final data in ascending order. For each of the 14 letters which participate in the Qur’anic initials, the following three values were de-termined: 1. The Absolute Frequency: This was simply the number of occurrences of each letter in each sura. 2. The Percentage of Frequency: This value was calculated by dividing the frequency of occurrence of each letter by the total number of letters in the sura, then multiplying the product by 100. 3. The Average Per Verse Value: This was determined by dividing the absolute frequency of a given letter by the number of verses which constitute the sura. For a multi-lettered set of Qur’anic initials, these three values were determined by adding up the corresponding values of all the constituent letters.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Thus, the absolute frequency values were added together, the percentage values were added together, and the average per verse values were added together. To illustrate, let us consider sura Al-Baqara. This sura is made up of 286 verses, with the first verse consisting of three alphabetic letters, Alif Lām Mīm (A.L.M.). The total number of letters in this sura is 25,717. The absolute frequency of occurrence of the letter Alif (A) is 4,329. This makes the percentage value of the letter Alif (A) in sura Al-Baqara = (4,329/25,717) x 100 = 16.8%. The average per verse
segments.label: page

segments.text: occurrence of the letter Alif (A) in sura Al-Baqara would be 4,329/286 = 15.14. The corresponding values for the letter Lām (L) are 2,941, 11.4%, and 10.28. For the letter Mīm (M), the three values were determined as 2,195, 8.5%, and 7.67, respectively. Thus, the absolute frequency value for the set of initials Alif Lām Mīm (A.L.M.) was determined by adding 4,329 + 2,941 + 2,195 = 9,465. Similarly, the percentage value of ALM in sura Al-Baqara was determined by adding 16.8 + 11.4 + 8.5 = 36.7%. The average per verse value of ALM in Al-Baqara was calculated as 15.14 + 10.28 + 7.67 = 33.09. Of course, all these computations were carried out by the computer. The three values for each one of the Qur'anic initials in each one of the 114 suras were thus determined.
segments.label: page

segments.text: The reason for following this particular method for calculation of the multi-lettered Qur'anic initials is the assertion by Prophet Muḥammad (peace be upon him) that their constituent letters are independent of each other. This was in a ḥadīth reported by Al-Bukhāry, Al-Bayḍawy, and Al-Suyūṭy. The Prophet said, "I do not say that Alif Lām Mīm (A.L.M.) constitutes one entity. I say that Alif (A) is an independent letter, Lām (L) is an independent letter, and Mīm (M) is an independent letter." The following data were fed into the computer: 1. The computer printouts of all the lists are shown within the text, and will be referred to as required. In searching for a single value which will represent each one of the Qur’anic initials most accurately, the percentage value stands out as the best possible choice. Certainly, we cannot use the absolute frequency of occurrence of a given letter, or a set of letters, as a representative measure or as a basis for comparing the various suras. For example, we cannot compare a long sura such as Al-Baqara (286 verses, 25,717 alphabetic 39
segments.label: page

segments.text: letters), with a short sura such as Al-Nās (3 verses, 99 alphabetic letters) on the basis of absolute frequency of occurrence. Similarly, the average per verse value cannot be used as a truly representative measure of the frequency of occurrence of the Qur'anic initials. The percentage value, therefore, appears to be the only value which can be used as a basis for comparison. However, we will have to take into consideration that the percentage value does not ALWAYS offer a good representation of the frequency value. It can be distorted by such factors as the lack of sufficient component units (statistically known as observations). To illustrate this point, let us take the extreme example of a chapter which consists of only the two letters A and B. The percent of each of these letters would be 50%, an extraordinarily high percentage value.
segments.label: page

segments.text: If we compare the letter A in each chapter of the book, the hypothetical two-lettered chapter undoubtedly will have the highest percentage value (50%). But we cannot honestly conclude from this comparison that this two-lettered chapter "has the highest frequency of the letter A." In this study, we will come across instances where the percentage value is obviously distorted by the extreme shortness of certain suras. Whenever the percentage value is questionable (as a true representative of the frequency), we will have to consider carefully all three values of the Qur'anic initial under study (the absolute number, the percentage, and the average per verse value). These instances and the computations involved in them will be discussed in detail wherever the occasion arises in the text. 40
segments.label: page

segments.text: Additionally, since different letters make up different sets of Qur’anic initials, we do not expect all the initials to exhibit one and the same phenomenon (e.g. the frequency of occurrence). Thus all three values may be needed under certain circumstances as we study the Qur’anic initials. 41

segments.text: Careful examination of these three suras reveals that they are extremely short. This fact raises the possibility that the percentage value of Qāf might be distorted out of true representation of frequency due to the extreme shortness of these suras. This type of statistical distortion was explained on page 40. Furthermore, the careful examination reveals that all three suras are vastly inferior to sura Qāf in the overall frequency value of the letter Qāf (Q). Thus, both the absolute frequency of Qāf (Q), and the average per verse value are lower in these three suras than in sura Qāf. Table 13 is a computer printout of the absolute frequency values of Qāf, and Table 14 is a computer printout of the average per verse values of Qāf throughout the Qur'an.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Table 15 shows the detailed determination of the overall frequency of the letter Qāf in sura Qāf, and in the three short suras exhibiting a higher percentage of Qāf. We note from Tables 13 and 15 that sura Al-Shams (The Sun) contains a total of 10 Qāfs compared to 57 in sura Qāf. Similarly, we note that sura Al-Qiyāma (Resurrection) contains 27 Qāfs (Q's), and sura Al-Falaq (Daybreak) contains but 6 Qāfs. | Sura | Absolute Number | Difference | Percent Value | Difference | Avg./ Verse | Difference | Net | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Qāf | 57 | 0 | 3.782 | 0 | 1.267 | 0 | 0 | | Al-Shams | 10 | -4.700 | 3.906 | +0.033 | 0.667 | -0.899 | -5.566 | | Al-Qiyāma | 27 | -1.100 | 3.907 | +0.033 | 0.675 | -0.877 | -1.944 | | Al-Falaq | 6 | -8.500 | 6.667 | +0.763 | 1.200 | -0.056 | -7.793 |

segments.text: From Tables 14 and 15 we note that the average per verse value of the letter Qāf in sura Qāf is 1.267. The corresponding value in sura Al-Shams is 0.667; in sura Al-Qiyāma it is 0.675, and in sura Al-Falaq it is 1.200. The net OVERALL frequency, derived from all three values of the letter Qāf in the four suras, is presented in Table 15. The computation was carried out by determining the magnitude of difference above and/or below sura Qāf with regard to each one of the three values, in each sura. The magnitude of difference was computed by deducting the smaller value from the larger value, then dividing the difference by the smaller value. A plus sign would indicate that the difference is above the reference sura (sura Qāf in this case), and a minus sign would indicate that the difference is below the reference sura.
segments.label: page

segments.text: To illustrate, let us compare sura A which contains 75 occurrences of a given letter with sura B which contains 25 occurrences of the same letter. The magnitude of difference in this case equals (75-25)/ 25 = 2.000. If sura A were the reference sura, a plus sign should precede the magnitude of difference (+2.000). This means that the absolute frequency of the letter in question is higher in sura A than in sura B by a two-fold magnitude. If sura B were the reference sura, a minus sign would precede the 2.000. By comparing the net overall frequency of the letter Qāf in sura Qāf with the overall frequency in the three suras exhibiting a higher percentage value, we note that sura Qāf is actually more than 5 times greater than
segments.label: page

segments.text: sura Al-Shams, almost two times greater than sura Al-Qiyāma, and more than 7 times greater than sura Al-Falaq (see Table 15). These observations lead us to the conclusion that the only three suras in the Qur'an which exhibit a higher percentage of Qāf than that in sura Qāf are in fact inferior to sura Qāf in the overall frequency. This means that SURA QĀF CONTAINS THE HIGHEST FREQUENCY OF THE LETTER QĀF THAN ANY OTHER SURA IN THE QUR'AN. What does this startling observation mean? For one thing, it means that someone knew that a particular sura will have the highest overall frequency value of the letter Qāf. To indicate this knowledge, this particular sura was "tagged" with the letter Qāf, and also entitled "Qāf." The next logical question would be, "Who is that 'SOMEONE'?" Who could possibly acquire advance knowledge about the distribution of the alphabet throughout the Qur'an?
segments.label: page

segments.text: As we ask these questions, we should bear in mind that the Qur'an was revealed over a period of 23 years, and that the verses within each sura were often widely separated both in time and place. It takes little thinking to realize that ONLY GOD ALMIGHTY can acquire such knowledge. Perhaps this explains to us the wisdom behind revealing the Qur'an in this particular fashion, coupled with deliberate concealment of the significance of the Qur'anic initials. This point will be explained in detail in the Epilogue section of this book. Within sura Qāf, one verse, namely, verse number 38, was revealed in Medina, more than 300 miles
segments.label: page

segments.text: and many years away from other verses of this Meccan sura. Yet, this one verse contains two Qāfs, a higher than average occurrence (as we know, the average per verse value of the letter Qāf in sura Qāf is 1.267). The only alternative to this conclusion would identify that "SOMEONE" as the Prophet Muḥammad (peace be upon him). This alternative conclusion, however, will have to assume that the Prophet, an illiterate man, had an advance knowledge of the distribution pattern of the letter Qāf and its exact proportions throughout 114 chapters to be revealed in scattered verses over the next 23 years. The reader can easily see the farfetchedness of such a conclusion. And we are yet talking about only one, the first, of 14 Qur'anic initials. Even without going any further in this study, we already have sufficient evidence that ONLY GOD COULD BE THE AUTHOR OF QUR'AN.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Lest someone may actually claim that the mathematical superiority of sura Qāf in the overall frequency value of the letter Qāf is coincidental, God Almighty provided further evidence supporting the observed superiority. Thus, the only other sura in the Qur'an which bears the letter Qāf as a Qur'anic initial, namely, sura Al-Shūrā (Consensus; No. 42), contains 57 Qāfs. This is the same frequency of occurrence found in sura Qāf (see Table 13). Furthermore, when we add the 57 Qāfs of sura Qāf plus the 57 Qāfs of sura Al-Shūrā, the product is 114, same as the total number of suras in the Qur'an. If the letter "Q" stands for "Qur'an," we have in these
segments.label: page

segments.text: two Qāf-initialed suras one Qāf for each sura. The clear message here is that all 114 suras constitute the Qur'an, the whole Qur'an, and nothing but the Qur'an. The importance of this observation, and all the other observations in this study, is the fact that anyone can SEE them for himself. No guesswork or speculation is involved. Thus, anyone anywhere in the world can pick up a copy of the Qur'an, and count the letter Qāf in sura Qāf and in sura Al-Shūrā, the only suras initialed with the letter Qāf. This process which takes no more than 30 minutes would unveil the physical, factual, observation that these two suras contain the same number of Qāfs (Q's), 57. In just 30 minutes, anyone in the world can obtain for himself this observation which is no less significant than the previous observation concerning overall mathematical superiority.
segments.label: page

segments.text: In just 30 minutes, anyone in the world can SEE FOR HIMSELF physical evidence that the Qur'an is God's unaltered word. In these two Qāf-initialed suras, the presence of one more word (or one less) such as Qul (say), or Ḥuq (truth), or Qawm (folk), or any substitutions or alterations thereof during the past 14 centuries would have nullified this significant observation. 71 Qāf, Al-Shūrā, Qāf, Q's, Qul, Ḥuq, Qawm

segments.text: 2. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Nūn (N): 2. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Nūn (N): This initial occurs in one sura entitled Al-Qalam (The Pen). It is sura number 68 in the recorded sequence of suras; number 2 in the chronological sequence of revelation. Tables 16, 17, and 18 are the computer printouts of the percentage values of Nūn (N), the absolute frequency of occurrence values, and the average per verse values in all suras, respectively. The suras are arranged in ascending order with regard to these values. By looking at the list of percentage values of Nūn (Table 16), we note that sura Al-Qalam has a very high percentage of Nūn (N). It occupies position number 109 out of the 114 listings. This means that sura Al-Qalam (The Pen), which is initialed with the letter Nūn, has the highest percentage of Nūn, with the exception of only 5 suras.
segments.label: page - 2. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Nūn (N):

segments.text: However, careful examination of these five suras reveals that three of them are suras which contain Qur'anic initials. These three suras are Al-Shu'arā' (Poets), Al-Dukhān (Air Pollution), and Al-Ḥijr (The Ḥijr Valley). The Qur'anic initials which prefix these suras are Ṭā Sīn Mīm (Ṭ.S.M.), Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.), and Alif Lām Rā (A.L.R.), respectively. Moreover, we note that all three suras belong to "groups" of suras which bear identical Qur'anic initials. Thus, sura Al-Shu'arā' belongs to the Ṭā Sīn Mīm group which includes sura Al-Qaṣaṣ (History). Sura Al-Dukhān belongs to the Ḥa Mīm group which includes six other sister suras (see Tables 4, 5, and 6). Sura Al-Ḥijr has 4 sister suras which bear the initials Alif Lām Rā. As this study progresses, we will Nūn (ن), Al-Qalam (القلم), Al-Shu'arā' (الشعراء), Al-Dukhān (الدخان), Al-Ḥijr (الحجر), Ṭā Sīn Mīm (طسم), Ḥā Mīm (حم), Alif Lām Rā (الر), Al-Qaṣaṣ (القصص)
segments.label: page - 2. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Nūn (N):

segments.text: find that the suras with identical initials must be treated as one unit, as if they were one continuous sura. When we combine the three suras under study here with their sister suras, we note that the average percentage of the letter Nūn in the unified groups is indeed inferior to the percentage contained in sura Al-Qalam. These averaging computations are shown in Table 19. We already note that the mathematical superiority of sura Al-Qalam with regard to its initial (Nūn), is not as strong as that of sura Qāf with regard to the letter Qāf. We also note that while sura Qāf is entitled “Qāf” in addition to having Qāf as a Qur’anic initial, this is not the case with sura Al-Qalam. This Nūn-initialed sura is not entitled “Nūn.” One expects the different Qur’anic initials to exhibit different characteristics.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Thus, we find the requirement for averaging the suras with identical initials in the case of Nūn (N). As the reader recalls, no such averaging was required to see the superiority of the Qur’anic initial Qāf. It is through this diversity, and precision, that the miracle of the Qur’an becomes manifest as this study proceeds. Also, this phenomenon provides us with a possible answer to the question, “Why do certain suras bear identical initials?” After satisfying the requirement for averaging percent Nūn (N) in the sister suras which contain the initials Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Ḥā Mīm, and Alif Lām Rā, we note that only two suras in the whole Qur’an contain a higher percentage of Nūn than sura Al-Qalam. These two suras are Al-Ṣaffāt (The Lineup), and Al-Wāqi‘a (The Inev- Nūn, Qāf, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Ḥā Mīm, Alif Lām Rā, Al-Ṣaffāt, Al-Wāqi‘a
segments.label: page

segments.text: itable). Yet, by studying Table 18, we note that both suras are inferior to sura Al-Qalam in the average per verse occurrence of the letter Nūn. While sura Al-Qalam contains on the average 2.558 Nūns (N's) in each verse, sura Al-Ṣāffāt contains an average 2.385 Nūns per verse, and sura Al-Wāqi‘a contains an average 2.014 Nūns in each verse. Thus, the mathematical superiority of the Nūn-initialed sura (Al-Qalam) with regard to the frequency of the letter Nūn is unquestionable. After satisfying the requirement for averaging the percentage value of Nūn in the suras with identical initials, we find that THERE IS NOT ONE SURA IN THE WHOLE QUR'AN WHERE ALL THREE VALUES OF NŪN ARE HIGHER THAN THEIR COUNTERPARTS IN THE NŪN-INITIALED SURA, AL-QALAM.

segments.text: 3. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Ṣād (Ṣ): 3. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Ṣād (Ṣ): This initial occurs in two suras which were revealed consecutively, but separated in the recording sequence. The first sura is entitled “Ṣād (Ṣ),” and it ranks 38 both in the revelation order and recording order. The second sura is Al-A‘rāf (The Purgatory) which ranks 39 in the revelation sequence, and 7 in the order of recording. Sura Ṣād has the letter Ṣād as the only initial, while sura Al-A‘rāf bears three other letters as Qur'anic initials, namely, Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād (A.L.M.Ṣ.). The computer printouts of the percentage values of the letter Ṣād, its absolute frequency of occurrence values, and its average per verse values, are shown in Tables 20, 21, and 22, respectively. By examining the list of percentage values, the reader will note that sura Ṣād ranks 88 out of the 114 suras.
segments.label: page - 3. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Ṣād (Ṣ):

segments.text: Further examination reveals that the suras which exhibit a higher percentage of Ṣād than sura Ṣād are all, without exception, very short suras. This fact is illustrated in Table 23 which lists these suras and their content of the letter Ṣād. For sure, by studying the three computer listings (Tables 20, 21, and 22), we note that THERE IS NOT ONE SURA IN THE WHOLE QUR'AN WHERE ALL THREE VALUES OF THE LETTER ṢĀD ARE HIGHER THAN THEIR COUNTERPARTS IN SURA ṢĀD. As previously illustrated on page 40, the extreme shortness of these suras may contribute to a distortion of their percentage values beyond true representation of the frequency. This warrants a detailed look at the 82 ص
segments.label: page - 3. THE QUR'ANIC INITIAL Ṣād (Ṣ):

segments.text: different values of Ṣād in each one of these short suras. The overall frequency value of the letter Ṣād and the net magnitudes of difference in relation to sura Ṣād have been computed as explained on page 68. The results are shown in Table 24. This table shows that there are three suras which carry a plus sign, i.e., they are superior to sura Ṣād in the net overall frequency of the letter Ṣād. Therefore, although sura Ṣād contains a very high relative frequency of the letter Ṣād, its superiority is not absolute. It has the highest overall frequency of the letter Ṣād than any other sura in the Qur'an, with the exception of the three suras indicated in Table 24, namely, Al-Ḥashr (The Thronging), Al-Mulk (Kingship), and Al-ʿAṣr (The Afternoon).
segments.label: page

segments.text: These data remind us that the letter Ṣād, as a Qur'anic initial, covers not only sura Ṣād, but also sura Al-Aʿrāf (The Purgatory) which is a continuation of sura Ṣād as far as the letter Ṣād is concerned (chronologically, these two suras rank 38 and 39. See Tables 3 and 6). The percentage of the letter Ṣād is 0.954 in sura Ṣād, and 0.688 in sura Al-Aʿrāf. The average of these two values is 0.821%. Using this average, all suras with a higher than 0.821 percentage of Ṣād were studied in detail as shown in Table 25. All three values of Ṣād in these suras were considered, and the magnitudes of difference above and below the corresponding average of (sura Ṣād + sura Al-Aʿrāf) were computed as explained previously. As it turned out, only one sura, Yūsuf (Joseph), exhibited a plus sign for the net overall frequency of Ṣād (see Table 25). But sura
segments.label: page

segments.text: Yūsuf itself is an initialed sura which belongs to the Alif Lām Rā group (see Table 4). When this sura is considered with its sister suras, we find that the average percentage of Ṣād is indeed lower than in sura Ṣād or sura Al-A‘rāf (Table 26). Thus, by averaging the percentage value of Ṣād in the five A.L.R.-suras, we observe that the letter Ṣād has its highest relative frequency in the united suras Ṣād/Al-A‘rāf which are initialed with the letter Ṣād. This observation teaches us that the existence of the letter Ṣād as a Qur'anic initial in sura Al-A‘rāf is no accident. WE LEARN THAT EVERY SINGLE LETTER IN THE ENTIRE QUR'AN WAS CAREFULLY MEASURED AND CALCULATED. As we saw from these data, sura Ṣād by itself did not exhibit absolute superiority with regard to the initial Ṣād. We were unable to ignore the continuation of the Qur'anic initial Ṣād into the subsequent sura entitled Al-A‘rāf. Since sura Al-A‘rāf contains three other initials besides Ṣād, namely, Alif (A), Lām (L), and Mīm (M), a detailed discussion of this sura will follow later. 84

segments.text: 4. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Hā (Ṭ.H.): 4. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Hā (Ṭ.H.): This set of initials occurs in one sura whose title consists of the same two letters. Sura Ṭā Hā is the twentieth chapter in the recording order of Qur'an, while its chronological order of revelation is 45. The percentage occurrence of Ṭā Hā, the absolute frequency of occurrence, and the average occurrence per verse values are shown in Tables 27, 28, and 29, respectively. We note from the percentage list that sura Ṭā Hā clearly has a very high relative frequency of the letters Ṭā Hā. To find out what special characteristics sura Ṭā Hā might have with regard to its Qur'anic initials, a closer look at the suras with higher percentages of Ṭā Hā is warranted. Computation of the overall frequency value of Ṭā Hā was carried out for these suras, and the results are shown in Table 30.
segments.label: page - 4. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Hā (Ṭ.H.):

segments.text: We note from this table that five suras are superior to sura Ṭā Hā in the overall frequency value of the letters Ṭā Hā. These five suras are Al-Ḥajj (Pilgrimage), Al-Nūr (The Light), Al-Fat-ḥ (Victory), Al-Mujā-dala (The Argument), and Al-Tawba (Repentance). But we also note that all these five are Medinan suras. No Meccan sura is superior to sura Ṭā Hā in the overall frequency of the letters Ṭā Hā. For sure, by examining the three computer listings in Tables 27, 28, and 29, we find that there is not one Meccan sura in the whole Qur'an where all three values of Ṭā Hā are higher than their counterparts in sura Ṭā Hā. From these data, therefore, we observe that SURA ṬĀ HĀ IS SUPERIOR TO ALL MECCAN SURAS with Ṭā Hā
segments.label: page - 4. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Hā (Ṭ.H.):

segments.text: regard to the Qur'anic initials Ṭā Hā. The reader is reminded that sura Ṭā Hā is a Meccan sura. Together with later data in this study, this set of initials serves to confirm for us the location of revelation of the various suras. This conclusion will be discussed in detail elsewhere. We should also note that the letter Hā occurs as an initial in sura Maryam which precedes sura Ṭā Hā, both in the recording sequence and the chronological sequence. However, combining the values of Hā in these two suras does not impart any changes on the final results or conclusions. 96 Ṭā Hā, Hā, Maryam

segments.text: 5. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Yā Sīn (Y.S.): 5. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Yā Sīn (Y.S.): This set of initials occurs in one sura whose title is also Yā Sīn (Y.S.). Sura Yā Sīn ranks 36 in the recorded sequence of the Qur'an; 41 in the chronological sequence of revelation. The percentage values of Yā Sīn, the absolute frequency values, and the average per verse values, throughout the Qur'an, are shown in Tables 31, 32, and 33, respectively. Although this book may not make use of certain data and/or tables presented here, the data are provided in hopes that many other people will use them eventually to discover new facts relating to the miraculous composition of the Qur'an. Undoubtedly, this book only scratches the surface; merely uncovers the tip of a huge iceberg. Scholars who are much more versed in mathematics than this author may reach better methods of computation and/or value representation.
segments.label: page - 5. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Yā Sīn (Y.S.):

segments.text: Therefore, all the raw data are included in this book. When we look at Table 31, we note right away that sura Yā Sīn has an extremely low relative frequency of the two letters Yā Sīn (Y.S.). The only suras in the whole Qur'an which contain a lower percentage of Yā Sīn are five extremely short suras. These five suras are Al-'Aṣr (The Afternoon), Al-Falaq (Daybreak), Al-Kawthar (Bounty), Al-Shams (The Sun), and Al-Kāfirūn (The Disbelievers) (see Table 31). The total number of alphabetic letters in these five suras are 90, 90, 61, 256, and 114, respectively. As illustrated on page 40, this extreme shortness leads to distortion of the percentage يٰس
segments.label: page - 5. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Yā Sīn (Y.S.):

segments.text: value as a statistically representative value for the frequency of occurrence. It appears, therefore, that the special significance of sura Yā Sīn is that it has the lowest relative frequency of the letters Yā Sīn. This is of course a complete reversal of the observations made so far about the Qur'anic initials. It may be relevant here to note that the initials Yā Sīn themselves represent a reversal in the alphabetical sequence. The first letter in this set of Qur'anic initials, Yā, is the LAST letter of the Arabic alphabet (see Table 1). The letter Sīn, on the other hand, is a relatively early letter in the alphabetical sequence. When we survey the other Qur'anic initials, we find that the first two initials usually consist of an early letter in the common sequence of the Arabic alphabet, followed by a late letter.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Thus, we observe this pattern in the Qur'anic initials Ṭā→Hā, Ḥā→Mīm, Alif→Lām Mīm, Alif→Lām Rā, Alif→Lām Mīm Ṣād, Alif→Lām Mīm Rā, Kāf→Ḥā Yā ‘Ayn Ṣād, and Ḥā→Mīm ‘Ayn Sīn Qāf. Only Yā←Sīn, and Ṭā←Sīn represent a reversal of this pattern. We have seen in this section that the mathematical superiority phenomenon is reversed as far as the initials Yā Sīn in sura Yā Sīn are concerned. We shall see later that the initials Ṭā Sīn and Ṭā Sīn Mīm also exhibit unique mathematical phenomena. It should be pointed out, however, that although the common arrangement for the Arabic alphabet is the one shown in Table 1, as well as in Webster’s New Collegiate Dictionary, there have been different arrangements 105 Yā Sīn, Yā, Sīn, Ṭā, Hā, Ḥā, Mīm, Alif, Lām, Rā, Ṣād, Kāf, ‘Ayn, Qāf, Ṭā Sīn, Ṭā Sīn Mīm
segments.label: page

segments.text: during the ancient, pre-Qur'anic times. The observation concerning alphabet reversals in Yā Sīn, therefore, may be challenged by certain critics. In any case, this particular observation, or lack of it, has no effect whatsoever on the mathematical properties of sura Yā Sīn. 106

segments.text: 6. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.): 6. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.): This set of Qur'anic initials occurs in seven Meccan suras which are recorded consecutively (40 through 46), and were revealed consecutively (60 through 66). These seven suras are Ghāfir (Forgiver), Fuṣṣilat (Elucidated), Al-Shūrā (Consensus), Al-Zukhruf (Vanities), Al-Dukhān (Air Pollution), Al-Jāthiya (Amenability), and Al-Aḥqāf (The Dunes). One of these suras, namely, Al-Shūrā (number 42), contains a second set of initials, namely, ‘Ayn Sīn Qāf (‘A.S.Q.), and will be studied in further detail later. The computer printouts of the percentage values of Ḥā Mīm throughout the Qur'an, the absolute frequency values, and the average per verse values are shown in Tables 34, 35, and 36. The three values for each of the seven Ḥā Mīm suras have been grouped together and averaged (Table 37).
segments.label: page - 6. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.):

segments.text: When we examine the list of percentage values we note that the seven Ḥā Mīm suras are scattered throughout the list. Obviously, not all the Ḥā Mīm suras are expected to exhibit mathematical superiority with regard to the letters Ḥā Mīm. What remains to be seen, therefore, is whether or not their average values exhibit any special mathematical patterns. The average percentage of Ḥā Mīm in the seven suras is 10.095 (Table 37). When we insert this average value in the percentage list we find that 33 out of the 114 suras have a higher percentage of Ḥā Mīm. Computation of the magnitudes of difference and the net overall frequency value of Ḥā Mīm were carried out for these Ḥā Mīm, ‘Ayn Sīn Qāf
segments.label: page - 6. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ḥā Mīm (Ḥ.M.):

segments.text: 33 suras. The results are shown in Table 38. Examination of this table leads to several interesting observations. Thus, we note that five suras have plus signs, i.e., they are superior to the united Ḥā Mīm suras in the net overall frequency of the letters Ḥā Mīm. These five suras are Hūd (Prophet Hūd), Al-Fat-ḥ (Victory), Al-Mumtaḥina (The Test), Al-Rūm (The Romans), and Al-Jumua‘a (Friday). Two of these are Meccan suras, and three are Medinan. But we note that the two Meccan suras (Hūd & Al-Rūm) are initialed, and that each one of them belongs to a group of suras which have identical initials. Thus, just as we grouped and averaged the Ḥā Mīm suras, it appears that we have to group and average the other sister suras as well. It should be pointed out that the only Qur'anic initials which exist in consecutive suras are Ḥā Mīm, Alif Lām Mīm, and Alif Lām Rā.
segments.label: page

segments.text: We see here that each one of these groups is represented, and required to be grouped and averaged. Thus, the Alif Lām Mīm group is represented by sura Al-Rūm, and the Alif Lām Rā group is represented by sura Hūd (see Table 38). We note here that the member suras in each one of these three groups are mathematically dependent on each other, if we are to observe any specific pattern. This fact provides us with one possible explanation for having identical initials prefixing certain suras. The Qur'anic initials, therefore, were not placed in their respective suras randomly. In this study of the initials Ḥā Mīm, we find it necessary to group and average the seven Ḥā Mīm suras, the six Alif Lām Mīm suras, and 113 Ḥā Mīm, Al-Fat-ḥ, Al-Mumtaḥina, Al-Rūm, Al-Jumua‘a, Hūd, Alif Lām Mīm, Alif Lām Rā
segments.label: page

segments.text: the five Alif Lām Rā suras. The average percentage of occurrence of Ḥā Mīm in each of these three groups is shown in Table 39. Having done this, we note that THERE IS NOT ONE SINGLE SURA IN THE WHOLE QUR'AN WHERE ALL THREE VALUES OF ḤA MĪM ARE HIGHER THAN THEIR COUNTERPARTS IN THE ḤA MĪM SURAS. We also note that if we exclude the average per verse values, the overall frequency values of the 33 suras analyzed in Table 38 are found lower than the overall frequency of Ḥā Mīm in the Ḥā Mīm suras. And, if we take all three values into consideration (i.e., including the average per verse value), we find that the ONLY suras which are superior to the Ḥā Mīm suras in the net overall frequency of Ḥā Mīm are Medinan suras. As shown in Table 38, these are the three Medinan suras Al-Fat-ḥ (no. 48), Al-Mum-taḥina (no. 60), and Al-Jumu‘a (no. 62).
segments.label: page

segments.text: Thus, we note here that the unified Ḥā Mīm suras are SUPERIOR TO ALL THE MECCAN SURAS in the overall frequency of the letters Ḥā Mīm. The reader is reminded that the seven Ḥā Mīm suras are Meccan. This mathematical feature, therefore, contributes to the confirmation of the location of revelation, just as we saw with the Ṭā Hā Qur'anic initials (page 96). 114 Ḥā Mīm, Alif Lām Rā, Al-Fat-ḥ, Al-Mum-taḥina, Al-Jumu‘a, Ṭā Hā

segments.text: 7. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn (Ṭ.S.): and 8. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn Mīm (Ṭ.S.M.) 7. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn (Ṭ.S.): and 8. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn Mīm (Ṭ.S.M.) This group of initials occurs in three suras which are consecutive both in the recording sequence and the chronological revelation sequence of Qur'an. Two suras are initialed with the three letters Ṭā Sīn Mīm. These are Al-Shu'arā' (Poets) and Al-Qaṣaṣ (History). The Qur'anic initials constitute an independent verse in these two suras. The two letters Ṭā Sīn occur in sura Al-Naml (The Ant), and they make up only part of the first verse, rather than an independent verse. The recording numbers of suras Al-Shu'arā' (Poets), Al-Naml (The Ant), and Al-Qaṣaṣ (History) are 26, 27, and 28, respectively. The revelation numbers of these three suras are 47, 48, and 49, respectively.
segments.label: page - 7. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn (Ṭ.S.): and 8. THE QUR'ANIC INITIALS Ṭā Sīn Mīm (Ṭ.S.M.)

segments.text: Thus, we have here three consecutive suras where the two-lettered set of Qur'anic initials separates the three-lettered sets of initials. There have been many discussions and speculations concerning the absence of Mīm from the Qur'anic initials of the middle sura, Al-Naml. The discussion presented by 'Abdullah Yūsuf 'Ali, and shown on page 27 of this book, is typical, and provides the reader with a good example of the literature treatment of this subject. Most books of tafsīr present similar theories regarding this Ṭā Sīn Mīm/Ṭā Sīn/Ṭā Sīn Mīm arrangement. 120 Ṭā Sīn, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Al-Shu'arā', Al-Qaṣaṣ, Al-Naml, tafsīr

segments.text: The computer printouts of the percentage values of Ṭā Sīn and Ṭā Sīn Mīm, their absolute frequency of occurrence values, and their average per verse values throughout the Qur'an are shown in Tables 40 through 45. When we look at the ascending order of percentage values of Ṭā Sīn Mīm (Table 40), we note that sura Al-Qaṣaṣ (History) ranks 36, and sura Al-Shu‘arā’ (Poets) ranks 79, out of the Qur'an's 114 suras. It takes little thinking to realize that exactly 35 suras have a higher percentage of Ṭā Sīn Mīm than that of sura Al-Shu‘arā’, and exactly 35 suras have a lower percentage of Ṭā Sīn Mīm than sura Al-Qaṣaṣ. Figure 3 clarifies this observation. The arrangement of the three Ṭā Sīn/Ṭā Sīn Mīm suras, both in revelation order and recording order, gives a special sense of balance, as can be seen in Figure 3.

segments.text: The observation that 35 suras contain a higher proportion of Ṭā Sīn Mīm than sura Al-Shu‘arā’, and the same number of suras contain a lower percentage than sura Al-Qaṣaṣ, leaves little doubt that the omission of Mīm in sura Al-Naml's Qur'anic initials was not coincidental. Let us also remember that the two Ṭā Sīn Mīm sets of initials form an independent verse each, while the Ṭā Sīn set which separates them does not make up an independent verse. The fact that this mathematical balance, manifested through the use of electronic computers, depends on the relative frequency of occurrence of Ṭā Sīn Mīm throughout the Qur'an is an undeniable evidence that the Qur'an could never be man-made, let alone man- Ṭā Sīn, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Al-Qaṣaṣ, Al-Shu‘arā’, Al-Naml, Mīm

The difference between the two suras is 615 - 580 = 35. This striking observation needs no further comment. The calculations and arrangement of information from the suras were all carried out by the computer, away from human bias. It would take the reader less than five minutes to count the number of suras above and/or below suras Al-Shu'arā' and/or Al-Qasas. It would take less than half an hour to count the letters Ṭā, Sīn, and Mīm in these two suras, and discover for one's self that the difference between them is exactly 35. Thus, the evidence that THE QUR'AN IS THE WORD OF GOD; the evidence that THE QUR'AN CAN NEVER BE MAN-MADE, is physical, touchable, and examinable evidence.

segments.text: The mathematical phenomena we just observed, are but one facet of the multi-dimensional miracle of the Qur'anic initials Ṭā Sīn/Ṭā Sīn Mīm. Thus, when we look at the list of percentage values of Ṭā Sīn, we note that sura Al-Naml (The Ant) which is initialed by Ṭā Sīn contains 2.533% of the letters Ṭā Sīn. To find out whether the suras with a higher percentage are genuinely superior in the overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn, the net overall frequency was computed as described on page 68. The results are shown in Table 46, and they reveal that only 3 suras have a higher overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn than 124
segments.label: page

segments.text: sura Al-Naml. The first among these three suras is sura Yūsuf (Joseph). But we note that this is an initialed sura which belongs to the Alif Lām Rā (ALR) group. When this sura is averaged with its sister suras as explained previously (page 72), the average percentage value of Ṭā Sīn falls below that of sura Al-Naml. The second sura among the three suras with higher percentage is Al-Isrā’ (The Night Journey). This Meccan sura exhibits a plus sign in front of the net overall frequency value of Ṭā Sīn (Table 46). This means that sura Al-Isrā’ is unquestionably superior to sura Al-Naml with regard to the Qur'anic initials Ṭā Sīn. The third sura with a higher percentage is sura Ṭā Hā. But this sura bears the initial Ṭā in common with sura Al-Naml. Therefore, the superiority of Ṭā Hā is nullified, since it is expected to, and does, have a high overall frequency in the letter Ṭā.
segments.label: page

segments.text: This leaves sura Al-Isrā’ as the only sura with a higher overall frequency than sura Al-Naml, with regard to the letters Ṭā Sīn. The final conclusion from this analysis is that SURA AL-NAML IS SUPERIOR TO ALL SURAS OF THE QUR'AN IN THE OVERALL FREQUENCY OF THE LETTERS ṬA SIN, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF SURA AL-ISRA'. This observation is quite significant, when we study the revelation position of sura Al-Isrā’. In the revelation sequence of Qur'an, we find that sura Al-Isrā’ falls between the Ṭā Sīn group of suras, and the Alif Lām Rā group (see Table 3). As we shall see later, sura Al-Isrā’ is also superior in the letters Alif Lām Rā, even over 125
segments.label: page

segments.text: the Alif Lām Rā suras themselves. Only three of the five Alif Lām Rā suras are recorded consecutively in a manner identical to that of the Ṭā Sīn group. One cannot help but observe the underlying sense of balance in these arrangements. Thus, we have three Ṭā Sīn suras which were revealed consecutively, and recorded consecutively. These three suras are Al-Shu‘arā’, Al-Naml, and Al-Qaṣaṣ. And we have three Alif Lām Rā suras which were revealed consecutively, and recorded consecutively. These suras are Yūnus, Hūd, and Yūsuf. These six suras which have in common the characteristic of being revealed and recorded consecutively are separated from each other by one sura, namely, Al-Isrā’. And it is the only sura which shows a higher frequency of Ṭā Sīn over the preceeding group, and also a higher overall frequency of Alif Lām Rā over the succeeding suras.
segments.label: page

segments.text: Can these factual observations be mere coincidence? The data herein deems a coincidence highly improbable. Increasingly, we are SEEING that every single word, indeed every single letter in the Qur’an is carefully calculated. As for the Ṭā Sīn Mīm suras, we have seen that 35 suras contain a higher percentage of Ṭā Sīn Mīm than sura Al-Shu‘arā’. When we calculate the magnitudes of difference in these 35 suras above and/or below sura Al-Shu‘arā’ (as described on page 68), we find that only 8 suras are actually higher than Al-Shu‘arā’ in the overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn Mīm. These suras are Al-Naml (The Ant), Hūd (Prophet Hūd), Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Muḥammad, Al-Rūm (The Romans), Al-Fat-ḥ (Victory).
segments.label: page

segments.text: Al-Zukhruf (Vanities), and Al-Jumu'a (Friday). Since sura Al-Naml is a member of the Ṭā Sīn group, it should be taken out of the comparison. This leaves seven suras with a higher overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn Mīm. Within these seven suras, we find all the multi-sura Qur'anic initials represented. Thus, the Alif Lām Rā group of suras is represented by suras Hūd and Ibrāhīm, the Alif Lām Mīm suras are represented by al-Rūm, and the seven Ḥā Mīm suras are represented by Al-Zukhruf (see Table 47). As shown in Table 48, when these four suras are joined with their respective sister suras, the average percentage of Ṭā Sīn Mīm is found clearly below that of sura Al-Shu'arā'. This leaves only three superior suras in the everall frequency of Ṭā Sīn Mīm. These are suras Muḥammad, Al-Fat-ḥ, and Al-Jumu'a. And we note that all three suras are Medinan.
segments.label: page

segments.text: The final observation, therefore, is that the Ṭā Sīn Mīm-initialed sura Al-Shu'arā', which is a Meccan sura, is superior to ALL MECCAN SURAS in the overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn Mīm. Even without combining the sister suras which contain identical initials, and without doing any further computations, the three computer printouts of the Ṭā Sīn Mīm values show that there is not one single sura in the whole Qur'an where all three values of Ṭā Sīn Mīm are higher than their counterparts in sura Al-Shu'arā'. One additional observation is the fact that if we disregard the average per verse value (Table 47), we find that sura Al-Shu'arā' has the highest overall frequency of Ṭā Sīn Mīm over all the suras, Meccan and Al-Zukhruf, Al-Jumu'a, Al-Naml, Ṭā Sīn, Ṭā Sīn Mīm, Alif Lām Rā, Hūd, Ibrāhīm, Alif Lām Mīm, al-Rūm, Ḥā Mīm, Al-Shu'arā', Muḥammad, Al-Fat-ḥ
segments.label: page

segments.text: Medinan. Sura Al-Qasas (History), on the other hand, cannot be mathematically superior in the frequency of Ta Sin Mim, since it has the low rank of 36 in the percentage list. It is possible that the fact that sura Al-Qasas balances sura Al-Shu'ara' (having 35 suras with a lower relative frequency as compared to 35 suras above sura Al-Shu'ara') is the sole mathematical phenomenon of sura Al-Qasas. To find out whether this is true or not, will require vast computations of the overall frequency values of sura Al-Qasas by itself and in combination with sura Al-Shu'ara'. Since the balance function of sura Al-Qasas, as illustrated in Figure 3, is quite sufficient for our purposes at this time, we will forsake such computations. This book by no means covers all the mathematical phenomena of the Qur'anic initials. It merely scratches the surface. 128
